meaning: The U.S. phone number for emergencies: police, fire and ambulance. Call for chest pain, stroke signs, trouble breathing, severe bleeding or someone who will not wake up.
The U.S. Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Call or text 988 any time, day or night, for free, private support. Help is available in many languages.
A blood test that shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months. It is used to find and manage diabetes. Also called HbA1c.
The belly: the part of the body between the chest and the hips that holds the stomach, intestines, liver and other organs.
Having to do with the belly (abdomen), such as abdominal pain.
A procedure that destroys a tiny area of tissue, often inside the heart, to stop it from causing an irregular heartbeat.
Not usual or not healthy. An abnormal test result is outside the normal range and may need a closer look.
A scrape: skin rubbed away by friction, like a scraped knee.
A pocket of pus under the skin or inside the body, caused by an infection. It is often swollen, red and painful.
A type of blood pressure medicine (such as lisinopril) that relaxes blood vessels. It can cause a dry cough in some people.
A common medicine for pain and fever (brand name Tylenol; called paracetamol in many countries). Taking too much can damage the liver.
When stomach acid comes back up into the food pipe, causing a burning feeling in the chest or throat (heartburn).
A skin condition with pimples, blackheads and bumps, most often on the face, chest and back.
Starting suddenly and usually lasting a short time. The opposite of chronic.
Being unable to stop using a substance (like alcohol or drugs) or doing an activity, even when it causes harm.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a condition that makes it hard to pay attention, sit still or control impulses.
Being formally checked into the hospital to stay overnight or longer.
Two small glands on top of the kidneys that make hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol.
A hormone the body releases under stress that speeds up the heart and breathing. Also given as a shot (epinephrine) for severe allergic reactions.
A legal document that says what medical care you want, or do not want, if you become too sick to speak for yourself.
Automated external defibrillator: a portable device that can check a stopped heart's rhythm and give an electric shock to restart it. It talks you through each step.
A U.S. law (ACA, or Obamacare) that created the Health Insurance Marketplace, where people can buy health insurance and may get help paying for it.
The most advanced stage of HIV infection, when the immune system is badly damaged. HIV treatment can prevent it.
Drinking alcohol. Heavy drinking raises the risk of liver disease, heart disease, high blood pressure and some cancers.
Something that causes an allergic reaction, such as pollen, peanuts, pet dander or certain medicines.
The body's response to something it is allergic to, such as hives, swelling, sneezing or, at worst, trouble breathing.
A doctor who treats allergies and asthma.
When the body's defense system overreacts to something usually harmless, causing sneezing, itching, rash, swelling or trouble breathing.
Tiny air sacs in the lungs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
A brain disease that slowly gets worse, causing memory loss, confusion and changes in thinking and behavior. The most common cause of dementia.
A vehicle with trained staff and equipment that takes sick or injured people to the hospital. In the U.S., call 911.
Able to walk. Ambulatory care means medical care where you visit and go home the same day.
Surgery to remove part or all of an arm, leg, finger or toe.
A pain reliever, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen.
A severe, sudden allergic reaction that can close the throat and drop blood pressure. It is an emergency: use an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) if you have one and call 911.
Not having enough healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen, which can make you tired, weak, pale or short of breath.
Medicine that stops you from feeling pain during surgery or a procedure. General anesthesia puts you to sleep; local anesthesia numbs one area.
A doctor who gives anesthesia and watches you during surgery.
A weak spot in a blood vessel wall that bulges like a balloon. It can be dangerous if it bursts.
Chest pain or pressure that happens when the heart is not getting enough blood, often during activity or stress.
An X-ray test that uses dye to show blood vessels and find blockages.
A procedure that opens a narrowed or blocked blood vessel, often using a tiny balloon and sometimes a small tube (stent).
A yearly checkup with your primary care doctor to review your health, update vaccines and order screening tests.
A medicine that calms heartburn and upset stomach by neutralizing stomach acid.
Something that reduces swelling and irritation (inflammation), such as ibuprofen.
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing. It works on bacterial infections, not on viruses like colds or flu. Finish the full course as prescribed.
When germs change so that antibiotics no longer kill them. Taking antibiotics only when needed, and finishing them as directed, helps prevent it.
A protein your body makes to recognize and fight germs. Vaccines help your body make antibodies.
A blood thinner: medicine that helps stop dangerous blood clots. It can make you bleed more easily.
A medicine used to treat depression and sometimes anxiety or pain.
A medicine that treats infections caused by fungus, such as athlete's foot or yeast infections.
A medicine for allergies that helps with sneezing, itching, runny nose and hives. Some kinds cause sleepiness.
A medicine, such as aspirin or clopidogrel, that keeps platelets from clumping and forming clots.
A medicine that treats infections caused by viruses, such as flu or COVID-19.
Strong worry, nervousness or fear. It becomes a health condition when it is hard to control and gets in the way of daily life.
The body's largest artery. It carries blood full of oxygen from the heart to the rest of the body.
A bulge in the wall of the aorta, the body's main artery. If it bursts it causes life-threatening bleeding. A screening ultrasound is offered to some older men who have smoked.
A tear in the inner wall of the aorta. It causes sudden, severe chest or back pain, often described as tearing. Call 911.
When the valve between the heart and the aorta becomes stiff and narrow, so the heart has to push harder to send blood out. It can cause chest pain, fainting or shortness of breath.
The heart valve that opens to let blood flow from the heart into the aorta, the body's main artery, and closes so it cannot flow back.
Trouble speaking, understanding, reading or writing, caused by damage to the brain, often from a stroke.
A blood thinner (brand name Eliquis) used to prevent strokes in atrial fibrillation and to treat clots.
Asking your insurance company to change its decision after it refuses to pay for a service or medicine.
Surgery to remove the appendix, usually because of appendicitis.
Swelling and infection of the appendix, a small pouch on the large intestine. It causes belly pain, often on the lower right, and usually needs surgery.
A scheduled time to see a doctor, nurse or other health worker.
An irregular heartbeat: the heart beats too fast, too slow or unevenly.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart to the body.
Swelling and pain in the joints, causing stiffness. It is common in older adults.
Surgery through small cuts using a tiny camera to look inside and repair a joint, such as the knee.
A medicine for pain, fever and swelling. A low daily dose is sometimes prescribed to help prevent heart attacks and strokes; ask a doctor first.
Housing for older adults who need some help with daily activities but not full nursing care.
A long-term lung condition where the airways narrow and swell, causing wheezing, coughing and trouble breathing.
Having no symptoms. You can have a condition or infection without feeling sick.
Hardening and narrowing of the arteries caused by fatty buildup (plaque) inside their walls. It is the main cause of heart attacks and strokes.
A common statin (brand name Lipitor) that lowers cholesterol.
A common irregular, often fast heartbeat (AFib). It raises the risk of stroke.
One of the two upper chambers of the heart. The atria collect blood coming back into the heart. Plural: atria.
A specialist who tests hearing and fits hearing aids.
A developmental condition that affects how a person communicates, interacts with others, and experiences the world.
A condition where the body's defense system attacks its own healthy cells by mistake, such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis.
Tiny living things. Some are helpful, but some cause infections that may need antibiotics.
A way to remember stroke signs: Balance loss, Eyes (vision loss), Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble, Time to call 911.
A sore on the skin from staying in one position too long, such as in bed or a wheelchair. Also called a pressure ulcer.
Not cancer and not spreading. A benign tumor is usually not life-threatening.
A non-cancerous enlarged prostate (BPH), common in older men. It can make it hard to pass urine or cause frequent trips to the bathroom.
A type of medicine (such as metoprolol) that slows the heart and lowers blood pressure. Do not stop taking it suddenly without asking your doctor.
On a prescription, means twice a day, often morning and evening.
On both sides of the body, such as both knees.
A bill from a doctor or hospital listing services and what you owe. Compare it with your Explanation of Benefits before paying.
Taking a small piece of tissue from the body to look at under a microscope, often to check for cancer.
A mental health condition with big mood swings, from very high energy (mania) to deep sadness (depression).
The stretchy bag in the lower belly that holds urine until you pass it.
Losing blood from a wound or inside the body. Press firmly on a bleeding wound with a clean cloth.
A full, tight or swollen feeling in the belly, often from gas.
A clump of blood that has turned from liquid into a gel. Clots stop bleeding from a cut, but a clot inside a blood vessel can block blood flow and cause a stroke or heart attack.
A test that checks a blood sample for bacteria or other germs growing in the blood.
Taking a sample of blood from a vein, usually in the arm, for lab tests.
Red, maroon or black, tarry stool. It can mean bleeding in the digestive tract and should be checked by a doctor.
A group of blood tests done on one sample, such as a metabolic panel or a lipid panel.
How hard your blood pushes against the walls of your arteries. Written as two numbers, like 120/80. High blood pressure strains the heart.
Medicine that lowers high blood pressure. Common types include ACE inhibitors, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics. Keep taking it even when you feel fine.
The amount of sugar (glucose) in your blood. It is the main thing checked and managed in diabetes.
Medicine that helps prevent dangerous blood clots. It can make you bruise or bleed more easily.
Giving a person blood or parts of blood from a donor through a vein.
Your blood group (A, B, AB or O, and positive or negative). It matters for blood transfusions.
A tube that carries blood around the body. Arteries, veins and capillaries are all blood vessels.
When things look fuzzy or out of focus. Sudden blurred vision can be a sign of stroke and needs urgent care.
Body mass index: a number from your height and weight used to estimate whether your weight is in a healthy range.
B-type natriuretic peptide: a blood test that is often high in heart failure.
A quick, low-dose X-ray (DEXA scan) that measures how strong your bones are. It checks for osteoporosis.
The soft, spongy tissue inside bones that makes blood cells.
An extra dose of a vaccine to keep protection strong.
The intestines: the long tube that food passes through after the stomach. The 'bowels' usually means the large intestine.
A heart rate that is slower than normal, usually under 60 beats a minute. It is normal in some athletes but can cause tiredness or fainting.
The lower part of the brain that connects to the spinal cord. It controls breathing, heartbeat and other automatic functions.
A medicine sold under the name the company that made it gave it. A generic version has the same active ingredient and usually costs less.
Cancer that starts in the breast. Mammograms help find it early.
Feeding a baby milk from the mother's breast. It gives the baby nutrients and helps protect against infections.
The two main airways that branch off the windpipe into the lungs.
A common lung infection in babies and young children that swells the small airways and makes breathing hard.
Swelling of the airways in the lungs, causing a cough that often brings up mucus.
A purple, blue or yellow mark on the skin from bleeding underneath, usually after a bump.
A bony bump at the base of the big toe that makes the toe lean toward the other toes.
Damage to the skin from heat, chemicals, electricity or the sun. Cool a minor burn under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes.
Being physically and emotionally worn out from long-term stress, often from work or caregiving.
Painful swelling of a small fluid-filled sac (bursa) that cushions a joint, often in the shoulder, elbow or hip.
Surgery that makes a new path for blood to flow around a blocked artery, often in the heart.
Cesarean section: delivering a baby through a cut in the mother's belly and uterus instead of through the vagina.
A type of medicine (such as amlodipine) that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure or treat chest pain. It can cause ankle swelling.
A unit for measuring the energy in food.
A disease where abnormal cells grow out of control and can spread to other parts of the body.
The tiniest blood vessels, thinner than a hair, where oxygen and food pass from the blood into the body's cells.
A medicine inside a small shell that dissolves in the stomach.
Carbs: sugars and starches in foods like bread, rice, fruit and sweets, which the body turns into glucose for energy.
Poisoning from a gas you cannot see or smell, from heaters, stoves or cars in closed spaces. It causes headache, dizziness and confusion. Get to fresh air and call 911.
Cancer that starts in the skin or in the lining of organs. It is the most common type of cancer.
Having to do with the heart.
When the heart suddenly stops beating. It is an emergency: call 911, start CPR, and use an AED.
A test where a thin, soft tube is passed through a blood vessel in the wrist or groin up to the heart, to look for blocked arteries or measure pressures.
A supervised program of exercise, education and support that helps people recover after a heart attack, heart surgery or heart failure.
A surgeon who operates on the heart, such as for bypass or valve surgery.
When the heart suddenly cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs, often after a major heart attack. It is a life-threatening emergency.
A doctor who specializes in the heart and blood vessels.
A disease of the heart muscle that makes it weak, thick or stiff, so it pumps blood less well.
Having to do with the heart and blood vessels.
A treatment that resets an irregular heartbeat back to a normal rhythm, using a controlled electric shock or medicine.
A written plan from your health care team that lists your health goals, treatments and next steps.
A person who helps care for someone who is sick, disabled or elderly. It can be a family member or a paid worker.
One of the two large arteries on each side of the neck that carry blood to the brain.
An ultrasound of the arteries in the neck to check for narrowing that could lead to a stroke.
Numbness, tingling or weakness in the hand caused by a squeezed nerve in the wrist.
Firm, rubbery tissue that cushions joints and gives shape to the nose and ears.
A nurse or social worker who coordinates your care, especially when you leave the hospital.
A hard covering, usually of plaster or fiberglass, that holds a broken bone still while it heals.
Clouding of the lens in the eye that makes vision blurry. Common with age and fixable with surgery.
Surgery to remove the cloudy lens of the eye and replace it with a clear artificial lens. It is common and usually quick.
A thin, flexible tube put into the body to drain fluid (like urine) or to give medicine.
A hole in a tooth caused by decay.
Complete blood count: a common blood test that counts red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
A condition where eating gluten (found in wheat, barley and rye) damages the small intestine.
A bacterial skin infection that makes the skin red, swollen, warm and painful. It needs antibiotics.
The narrow lower part of the uterus (womb) that opens into the vagina.
Free or reduced-cost care that many hospitals offer to people with low income. Ask the hospital's billing office for an application.
Strong medicines that kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. Side effects can include hair loss, nausea and tiredness.
Pain, pressure, squeezing or tightness in the chest. It can be a sign of a heart attack: call 911 if it is sudden, severe or spreads to the arm, jaw or back.
A very contagious virus that causes an itchy rash of blisters. A vaccine prevents it.
Feeling cold and shivering, often with a fever.
Children's Health Insurance Program: low-cost health coverage for children in families that earn too much for Medicaid but cannot afford private insurance.
A practitioner who treats back, neck and joint pain, mainly by adjusting the spine.
When something blocks the airway so a person cannot breathe, cough or speak. Call 911 and give abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver).
Surgery to take out the gallbladder, often because of gallstones.
A fatty substance in the blood. Too much 'bad' cholesterol (LDL) can clog arteries and raise the risk of heart disease.
Lasting a long time or coming back often, like diabetes or arthritis. The opposite of acute.
Long-term damage that slowly makes the kidneys work less well (CKD). Diabetes and high blood pressure are the most common causes.
Severe scarring of the liver from long-term damage, such as heavy drinking or hepatitis. The liver stops working well.
A request to your insurance company to pay for a health service you received.
A place to get medical care without staying overnight.
An antiplatelet medicine (brand name Plavix) that helps prevent clots, often after a stent.
A type of talk therapy (CBT) that helps you notice and change unhelpful thoughts and habits.
Problems with memory, thinking or decision-making that are more than normal for a person's age.
The percentage of a bill you pay after you have met your deductible. For example, with 20% coinsurance you pay $20 of a $100 bill.
A small, painful blister on or near the lips caused by a virus. Also called a fever blister.
Long periods of crying in a healthy baby, often in the evening, for no clear reason. It usually gets better by 3 to 4 months.
The large intestine: the last part of the digestive tract, which absorbs water and forms stool.
A test where a doctor uses a thin camera to look inside the large intestine, often to check for colon cancer.
Cancer of the colon or rectum. Screening with a colonoscopy or stool test is recommended starting at age 45.
A mild virus infection of the nose and throat, with a runny nose, sneezing and sore throat. Antibiotics do not help a cold.
A clinic that gives care to everyone, charging less to people with low income or no insurance. Many have interpreters.
A trusted local worker who helps people get health care, understand their care and find resources, often in their own language.
Having more than one health condition at the same time.
A new problem that happens because of an illness, treatment or surgery.
A blood test (CMP) that checks blood sugar, salts (electrolytes), kidney function and liver function.
A brain injury from a blow to the head, which can cause headache, confusion, dizziness or memory problems.
Trouble thinking clearly, paying attention or knowing where you are. Sudden confusion needs urgent care.
Present from birth.
A problem with the heart's structure that a baby is born with, such as a hole between chambers.
A stuffy, blocked feeling, often in the nose or chest.
Heart failure where fluid builds up in the lungs, legs or belly because the heart cannot pump well enough (CHF).
Pink eye: redness and swelling of the clear layer over the white of the eye, from infection or allergy. Some kinds spread easily.
A paper you sign to show you understand and agree to a treatment, test or surgery. You can ask questions before signing.
Having bowel movements less often than usual, or stools that are hard and difficult to pass.
Able to spread from one person to another.
A small sensor worn on the skin (CGM) that checks blood sugar all day and night and sends readings to a phone or reader.
Birth control: methods used to prevent pregnancy, such as pills, condoms, IUDs or implants.
Tightening of the uterus during labor. Regular contractions that get stronger and closer together mean labor has started.
A reason not to use a certain medicine or treatment because it could be harmful for you.
A liquid given by mouth or into a vein before some scans so that organs and blood vessels show up more clearly. Tell staff if you have kidney problems or allergies.
A fixed amount you pay for a doctor visit or medicine, with your insurance paying the rest.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a long-term lung disease that makes it hard to breathe, often caused by smoking.
The clear front layer of the eye that covers the colored part and the pupil.
The arteries that wrap around the heart and bring blood and oxygen to the heart muscle itself.
Narrowing of the blood vessels that feed the heart, usually from fatty buildup. It can lead to chest pain or a heart attack.
A strong anti-inflammatory medicine, such as prednisone. It can be a pill, cream, inhaler or shot. Long-term use has side effects.
Forcefully pushing air out of the lungs to clear the airways. A cough lasting more than three weeks should be checked by a doctor.
Talking with a trained professional to work through problems, feelings or stress.
The health services and medicines your insurance plan helps pay for.
An illness caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2. It can cause fever, cough, tiredness and loss of taste or smell, and can be serious for older adults.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: pressing hard and fast on the chest (and sometimes giving breaths) to keep blood flowing when someone's heart has stopped.
A sudden, painful tightening of a muscle that you cannot control.
A waste product in the blood that the kidneys remove. A high level can mean the kidneys are not working well.
A long-term disease that causes inflammation in the digestive tract, with belly pain, diarrhea and weight loss.
C-reactive protein: a blood test that shows inflammation in the body.
A test that uses X-rays and a computer to make detailed pictures of the inside of the body.
A bluish color of the skin or lips caused by not enough oxygen in the blood. It is a warning sign.
A closed sac under the skin or in the body that holds fluid, air or other material. Most are harmless.
Inflammation of the bladder, usually from a urinary tract infection. It causes burning when you pass urine.
A blood test used to help rule out a blood clot, such as a deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
On a food label, how much of a nutrient one serving gives compared with what most people need in a day.
An eating plan to lower blood pressure: lots of fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low-fat dairy, and less salt, sugar and red meat.
The amount you pay for health care each year before your insurance starts to pay.
A blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg (DVT). The leg may be swollen, warm and painful. The clot can break off and travel to the lungs.
A device that gives an electric shock to the heart to fix a dangerous rhythm. It can be outside the body (an AED) or placed under the skin (an ICD).
Slowly getting worse over time.
When your body loses more water than it takes in. Signs include thirst, dark urine, dizziness and a dry mouth.
Sudden confusion and trouble paying attention, often in older adults who are sick or in the hospital. It usually gets better when the cause is treated.
A loss of memory, thinking and reasoning that is bad enough to affect daily life. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause.
A doctor who cares for the teeth and gums.
A medical condition with long-lasting sadness or loss of interest, which can affect sleep, appetite, energy and thinking. It is treatable.
Irritated, inflamed skin that is red, itchy or swollen.
A doctor who specializes in skin, hair and nails.
Skills most children learn by a certain age, such as smiling, walking and talking.
A long-term condition where blood sugar is too high because the body does not make or use insulin well.
Nerve damage from diabetes, usually in the feet and legs. It causes numbness, tingling or pain, so foot injuries can go unnoticed.
Damage to the back of the eye caused by diabetes. It can lead to blindness, so people with diabetes need a yearly eye exam.
Identifying which illness or condition a person has.
A treatment that cleans the blood when the kidneys can no longer do it.
Red, sore skin in the diaper area.
The dome-shaped muscle under the lungs that you use to breathe.
Loose, watery stools happening more often than usual.
The bottom number in a blood pressure reading. It measures the pressure in the arteries while the heart rests between beats.
A trained expert in food and nutrition who can make an eating plan for your health.
The list of possible conditions a doctor considers before deciding which one you have.
1. Being officially sent home from the hospital. 2. Fluid that comes out of a part of the body, such as a wound.
When a bone is pushed out of its normal place in a joint, such as a shoulder.
A health condition where part of the body or mind does not work as it should.
Farther from the center of the body. The fingers are distal to the elbow.
A medicine that makes you pass more urine to remove extra water and salt from the body. Often called a water pill; used for high blood pressure and heart failure.
When small pouches in the wall of the colon become inflamed or infected, causing belly pain (usually lower left), fever and nausea.
Feeling lightheaded, faint, unsteady, or like the room is spinning.
Do not resuscitate: a medical order saying a person does not want CPR if their heart or breathing stops.
How much of a medicine to take and how often.
The amount of medicine you take at one time.
A covering, such as gauze or a bandage, put over a wound to protect it.
An allergic reaction to a medicine, such as penicillin. Always tell doctors and pharmacists about drug allergies.
When one medicine, food, drink or supplement changes how another medicine works. Tell your doctor and pharmacist everything you take.
Not having enough saliva. It is a common side effect of many medicines.
The date a baby is expected to be born, about 40 weeks after the first day of the last period.
Medical equipment for use at home, such as a wheelchair, walker, hospital bed or oxygen (DME). Insurance often helps pay with a prescription.
Trouble swallowing, or feeling that food gets stuck in the throat or chest.
The medical word for shortness of breath.
An infection in the ear, very common in young children, causing ear pain, fever and fussiness.
A serious condition with unhealthy eating habits and strong worry about weight or body shape, such as anorexia or bulimia.
An ultrasound of the heart. It uses sound waves to make moving pictures of the heart's chambers and valves. It does not hurt.
A skin condition that causes dry, itchy, red patches. It often starts in childhood.
Swelling caused by extra fluid trapped in the body, often in the feet, ankles or legs.
Electroencephalogram: a test that records the brain's electrical activity using small sensors on the scalp. It is used to check for seizures.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate: a number from a blood test that shows how well your kidneys filter blood. A lower number means weaker kidneys.
The share of blood the heart's main chamber pumps out with each beat. A normal number is about 50 to 70 percent; a lower number can mean heart failure.
Electrocardiogram (also ECG): a quick, painless test that records the heart's electrical activity using stickers on the skin.
Planned in advance and not an emergency, such as elective surgery.
Minerals in the blood, such as sodium, potassium and chloride, that help control fluid, muscles and heart rhythm.
Your medical record stored on a computer (EHR). Many clinics let you see it through an online patient portal.
A heart doctor who specializes in heart rhythm problems and devices like pacemakers.
A blockage in a blood vessel caused by something that traveled there in the blood, usually a blood clot.
Medicaid that pays only for emergency care. In many states it is available to people who do not qualify for full Medicaid, including some immigrants.
The part of a hospital (ER) for sudden, serious illness or injury. Open all day and night.
A lung disease, usually from smoking, where the air sacs are damaged and breathing becomes hard. It is a type of COPD.
Emergency medical technician: a trained worker who gives basic emergency care, often in an ambulance.
A U.S. law that says hospital emergency rooms must examine and stabilize anyone with an emergency, regardless of insurance, immigration status or ability to pay.
An infection of the inner lining of the heart or its valves. It is serious and needs treatment with antibiotics.
A doctor who treats hormone and gland problems, such as diabetes and thyroid disease.
When tissue like the lining of the uterus grows outside the uterus, causing painful periods and pelvic pain.
A test where a doctor uses a thin tube with a camera to look inside the body, often the throat and stomach.
Ear, nose and throat doctor, also called an otolaryngologist.
Explanation of Benefits: a statement from your insurance company showing what it paid and what you may owe. It is not a bill.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in a community or region.
A brain condition that causes repeated seizures.
A brand of epinephrine auto-injector: a pen-shaped shot used right away for a severe allergic reaction.
The food pipe: the tube that carries food and drink from the throat to the stomach.
The cause of a disease.
A flare-up: when a long-term condition suddenly gets worse.
Physical activity that makes your body work, such as walking, swimming or biking. Adults should aim for about 150 minutes a week.
The date after which a medicine may not work as well. Do not use expired medicine without asking a pharmacist.
A check of your vision and eye health. A dilated eye exam uses drops to widen the pupils so the doctor can see the back of the eye.
Passing out for a short time because not enough blood reaches the brain. Also called syncope.
How likely a person is to fall. Older adults, people on some medicines, and people with balance or vision problems have a higher fall risk.
A test result that says you do not have a condition when you really do.
A test result that says you have a condition when you really do not.
Health problems that run in your family, such as heart disease or diabetes. It can raise your own risk.
A primary care doctor who treats people of all ages.
Not eating or drinking anything except water for a set time, often 8 to 12 hours, before a blood test or procedure.
Feeling very tired or low on energy, even after rest.
A tube that carries liquid food directly into the stomach or intestine for people who cannot eat safely by mouth.
The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body.
A developing baby inside the uterus, from about 8 weeks of pregnancy until birth.
A body temperature higher than normal, usually 100.4°F (38°C) or above. Often a sign of infection.
The part of plant foods the body cannot digest. It helps digestion and can lower cholesterol and blood sugar.
A long-term condition with pain all over the body, tiredness, and trouble with sleep and memory.
Basic care given right away to someone who is hurt or suddenly sick, before professional help arrives.
A time when the symptoms of a long-term condition suddenly get worse.
Short for influenza: a virus that causes fever, body aches, cough and tiredness. A yearly flu shot helps prevent it.
A yearly vaccine that helps protect against influenza. It is recommended for almost everyone 6 months and older.
A B vitamin that helps prevent birth defects of the brain and spine. Women who could become pregnant are advised to take it daily.
A visit after a first visit, test or hospital stay to check how you are doing.
Illness from eating food or drink with germs or toxins in it, causing vomiting, diarrhea and stomach cramps.
Baby milk made from cow's milk or soy, used instead of or along with breast milk.
The list of prescription medicines your insurance plan covers.
A broken bone.
Being weak and less able to recover from illness or injury, common in older age.
Needing to pass urine more often than usual. It can be a sign of diabetes, infection or prostate problems.
Damage to skin and tissue from freezing, most often on fingers, toes, nose and ears.
A living thing, like yeast or mold, that can cause infections of the skin, nails or other body parts.
A strong water pill (brand name Lasix) that removes extra fluid, often used in heart failure. It makes you pass urine often.
A small pouch under the liver that stores bile, a fluid that helps digest fat.
Hard pieces that form in the gallbladder and can cause sharp pain in the upper right belly.
Death of body tissue because of lost blood supply or a serious infection. Diabetes and poor circulation raise the risk.
Inflammation of the stomach lining, causing upper belly pain, nausea or feeling full quickly.
Stomach flu: an infection of the stomach and intestines with vomiting and diarrhea. It is not the same as influenza.
A doctor who treats problems of the stomach, intestines, liver and digestion.
Medicine that puts you into a deep, sleep-like state during surgery so you feel nothing.
A medicine with the same active ingredient as a brand-name drug, usually much cheaper.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease: frequent acid reflux, where stomach acid often comes back up into the food pipe.
A doctor who specializes in the care of older adults.
A tiny living thing, such as a bacterium or virus, that can cause disease.
Diabetes that starts during pregnancy. It usually goes away after the baby is born but raises the risk of type 2 diabetes later.
An organ or group of cells that makes and releases substances such as hormones, sweat or saliva.
An eye disease, often from high pressure inside the eye, that can slowly damage vision. Regular eye checks catch it early.
Sugar in the blood. The body's main source of energy.
A small device that checks blood sugar from a drop of blood, usually from a finger prick.
A swelling at the front of the neck from an enlarged thyroid gland.
A type of arthritis that causes sudden, very painful swelling in a joint, often the big toe.
The deep sadness and other feelings that come after losing someone or something important.
A chart that tracks a child's height, weight and head size compared with other children the same age.
A doctor who treats women's reproductive health.
Seeing, hearing or feeling things that are not really there.
Washing your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. It is one of the best ways to prevent the spread of germs.
A common virus in young children that causes fever, mouth sores and a rash on the hands and feet.
CPR without mouth-to-mouth breaths: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute, until help arrives.
High-density lipoprotein, the 'good' cholesterol. It helps carry cholesterol away from the arteries, so a higher number is better.
Any injury to the scalp, skull or brain. Get emergency care for confusion, vomiting, passing out or a very bad headache after a head injury.
A person you choose to make medical decisions for you if you cannot make them yourself. Also called a health care agent or power of attorney for health care.
A plan that helps pay for medical care in exchange for a monthly payment (premium).
The government website (HealthCare.gov or your state's site) where you can compare and buy health insurance plans.
Not being able to hear as well as before. It is common with age; hearing aids can help.
A test that checks how well you hear different sounds and pitches.
When blood flow to part of the heart is blocked. Signs: chest pain or pressure, pain in the arm, jaw or back, shortness of breath, sweating. Call 911.
Chest pain or pressure, pain in the arm, back, neck or jaw, shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea or lightheadedness. Women may have less obvious signs. Call 911.
When the heart cannot pump blood as well as it should. It does not mean the heart has stopped. Causes tiredness, swelling and shortness of breath.
An extra whooshing sound a doctor hears through a stethoscope as blood flows through the heart. Many are harmless; some point to a valve problem.
How many times your heart beats in one minute. A normal resting rate for adults is about 60 to 100.
One of four flaps inside the heart that open and close to keep blood flowing in one direction.
A burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid coming up into the food pipe.
Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness and nausea from too much heat. Move to a cool place and drink water; it can turn into heat stroke.
A dangerous rise in body temperature from heat, with hot skin, confusion and possibly passing out. Call 911 and cool the person down.
Abdominal thrusts: quick, upward pushes just above the belly button to force out something blocking a choking person's airway.
The percentage of your blood made up of red blood cells. It is part of a CBC.
A doctor who treats blood disorders.
Blood in the urine. The urine may look pink, red or brown, or the blood may only show up in a test. It should be checked by a doctor.
The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Low hemoglobin is a sign of anemia.
Heavy bleeding, inside or outside the body.
Swollen veins around the anus or in the rectum that can itch, hurt or bleed.
Swelling of the liver, often caused by a virus (hepatitis A, B or C).
When enough people in a community are immune to a disease that it has trouble spreading, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
Passed down from parents to children through genes.
When an organ or tissue pushes through a weak spot in a muscle, often making a bulge in the belly or groin.
A common virus that causes blisters or sores, either around the mouth (cold sores) or on the genitals. It stays in the body for life.
Surgery that replaces a damaged hip joint with an artificial one.
A U.S. law that keeps your health information private and gives you the right to see your medical records.
Human immunodeficiency virus, which attacks the immune system. Daily medicine keeps it under control so people can live long, healthy lives.
Raised, itchy red bumps on the skin, often caused by an allergic reaction.
Health maintenance organization: an insurance plan where you usually must use doctors in its network and get a referral to see a specialist.
A rough, strained or weak voice.
A small recorder you wear for a day or more that records your heart's rhythm while you go about normal life.
Medical care given in your home, such as nursing or therapy, often after a hospital stay.
A chemical messenger made by the body that controls things like growth, mood, sleep and blood sugar.
Care focused on comfort, not cure, for people near the end of life, and support for their families.
A doctor who takes care of patients only while they are in the hospital.
Sudden feelings of heat in the face and body, often with sweating, common during menopause.
Human papillomavirus: a common virus spread by sexual contact that can cause warts and some cancers. A vaccine prevents it.
Having enough water in the body. Drink water through the day, especially in hot weather.
Having too much cholesterol in the blood (high cholesterol).
High blood sugar. It can cause thirst, frequent urination and tiredness.
High blood pressure. Often has no symptoms but raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease.
Blood pressure that is extremely high (about 180/120 or higher). With chest pain, headache, confusion or vision changes, it is an emergency.
An overactive thyroid that makes too much hormone, causing weight loss, a fast heartbeat, sweating and nervousness.
Low blood sugar. Signs include shakiness, sweating, confusion and hunger. Common in people treating diabetes.
Low blood pressure, which can cause dizziness or fainting.
A dangerously low body temperature, usually from being in the cold too long.
An underactive thyroid that does not make enough hormone, causing tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold and dry skin.
Surgery to remove the uterus (womb).
A common medicine for pain, fever and swelling (brands Advil, Motrin). Can upset the stomach; take with food.
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator: a small device put under the skin of the chest that watches the heart and shocks it if a dangerous rhythm starts.
Intensive care unit: a hospital area for very sick patients who need close, round-the-clock care.
Having no known cause.
The body's defense system that fights germs and disease.
Protection from a disease, usually by getting a vaccine.
Having a weakened immune system, from illness or medicine, so it is easier to get infections.
Treatment that helps the body's own immune system fight a disease such as cancer.
Doctors, hospitals and pharmacies that have a contract with your insurance plan. Using them usually costs you less.
A cut made by a surgeon during an operation.
Not being able to control when urine or stool leaves the body.
Discomfort or burning in the upper belly after eating, sometimes with bloating or nausea.
When germs such as bacteria or viruses enter the body and multiply, causing illness.
The body's response to injury or infection: redness, heat, swelling and pain.
The flu: a contagious virus causing fever, aches, cough and tiredness. A yearly vaccine helps prevent it.
Agreeing to a treatment after it has been explained to you, including its risks, benefits and other choices. You have the right to ask for an interpreter.
A small device that sprays medicine into the lungs, often used for asthma or COPD.
A shot: medicine given with a needle into the muscle, skin or vein.
A patient who stays in the hospital overnight or longer after being formally admitted.
A blood test that shows how long your blood takes to clot. It is used to check the dose for people taking warfarin.
Trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.
A hormone that moves sugar from the blood into the body's cells. People with diabetes may need insulin shots.
A pen-shaped device that holds insulin and lets you dial and inject a dose.
A plan you or your employer pays into that helps cover the cost of your health care.
The card from your health plan with your member ID and phone numbers. Bring it to every visit.
Paperwork you fill out at a first visit about your health, medicines and insurance.
A doctor of internal medicine who treats adults, often as a primary care doctor.
A trained person who translates spoken words between languages. Most U.S. hospitals must provide one for free if you ask.
The long tube from the stomach to the anus where food is digested and absorbed. It has a small intestine and a large intestine (colon).
IV: given through a vein, usually through a small tube in the arm.
A test or treatment that goes into the body through a cut or opening. For cancer, it means spreading into nearby tissue.
Not having enough iron in the body. It is the most common cause of anemia, making you tired and pale.
A common long-term condition (IBS) with belly pain, gas, bloating, diarrhea or constipation, without damage to the intestines.
When a part of the body does not get enough blood flow, and so not enough oxygen. Heart ischemia can cause chest pain.
Keeping a sick, contagious person apart from others so the illness does not spread.
A feeling on the skin that makes you want to scratch. The medical word is pruritus.
Intravenous line: a thin, soft tube put into a vein, usually in the hand or arm, to give fluids or medicine.
Yellowing of the skin and eyes, often a sign of a liver problem. Common and usually mild in newborns.
Pain in the jaw. With chest discomfort or shortness of breath, it can be a sign of a heart attack, especially in women.
A place where two bones meet, such as the knee, hip or elbow.
One of two bean-shaped organs that clean the blood and make urine.
When the kidneys can no longer clean the blood well enough. It is treated with dialysis or a kidney transplant.
A hard piece that forms in the kidney and can cause severe pain in the back or side when it passes.
Surgery that replaces a damaged knee joint with an artificial one.
The numbers and findings from your tests. Each result usually comes with a normal range; ask your doctor what yours mean.
A test on a sample of blood, urine or other body fluid to check your health.
The process of childbirth, when the uterus tightens (contractions) and the cervix opens so the baby can be born.
A deep cut or tear in the skin.
Trouble digesting the sugar in milk, causing gas, bloating or diarrhea after eating dairy.
Your right to free interpretation and translated documents at most U.S. hospitals and clinics. Ask for an interpreter; you do not have to rely on family members.
Surgery done through small cuts in the belly using a thin camera. Recovery is usually faster than with open surgery.
The voice box, at the top of the windpipe. It holds the vocal cords.
Toward the side of the body.
Low-density lipoprotein, the 'bad' cholesterol. Too much of it builds up in artery walls, so a lower number is better.
An area of damaged or unusual tissue, like a wound, sore or spot on the skin.
Feeling very sluggish, drowsy, or lacking energy.
A cancer of the blood and bone marrow.
Tiny insects that live in hair and cause itching. Common in school children and treated with special shampoos.
A tough band of tissue that connects one bone to another at a joint.
Feeling faint or like you might pass out.
A blood test that measures cholesterol and other fats in the blood.
A common blood pressure medicine (an ACE inhibitor) also used for heart failure and to protect the kidneys.
A large organ on the upper right side of the belly. It cleans the blood, helps digest food and stores energy.
A document that says what treatments you do or do not want at the end of life.
Medicine that numbs only a small part of the body. You stay awake.
Help with daily activities over a long time, at home or in a nursing home or assisted living facility.
Not feeling hungry or not wanting to eat.
Cancer that starts in the lungs. Smoking is the main cause.
The two organs in the chest that take in oxygen from the air and get rid of carbon dioxide.
An autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, such as the skin, joints and kidneys.
An infection spread by tick bites. It may start with a round, red 'bull's-eye' rash, fever and tiredness.
Small bean-shaped glands in the neck, armpits, groin and elsewhere that help fight infection. They often swell when you are sick.
A cancer of the lymph system, the part of the immune system that includes the lymph nodes.
An eye disease, common in older adults, that damages central vision, making it hard to read or see faces.
A general feeling of being unwell, tired or uncomfortable.
Cancerous: able to grow and spread to other parts of the body.
When the body does not get enough of the right food and nutrients to stay healthy.
An X-ray of the breast used to check for breast cancer.
Surgery to remove all or part of a breast, usually to treat breast cancer.
A very contagious virus that causes fever, cough and a rash all over the body. The MMR vaccine prevents it.
A U.S. government health insurance program for people with low income. Rules differ by state.
Information about your past and present health, illnesses, surgeries, medicines and family health.
A trained person who interprets between you and your health care team. Many hospitals must provide one for free.
The file that holds your health information, test results and treatments. You have the right to a copy.
A U.S. government health insurance program mainly for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities.
A Medicare plan run by a private insurance company (Part C) that combines Parts A and B and often Part D.
The part of Medicare that covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, hospice and some home health care.
The part of Medicare that covers doctor visits, outpatient care, preventive services and medical equipment.
The part of Medicare that helps pay for prescription medicines.
Medicine: a drug used to treat or prevent illness.
A written list of every medicine, vitamin and supplement you take, with doses. Bring it to every appointment.
An eating style with lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, fish and olive oil. It is linked to better heart health.
The most serious type of skin cancer. Watch for moles that change in size, shape or color.
Infection and swelling of the covering of the brain and spinal cord. Signs include fever, stiff neck and headache. It is an emergency.
When a woman's periods stop for good, usually around age 45 to 55.
Your emotional, psychological and social well-being: how you think, feel and cope with life.
A group of problems that together raise the risk of heart disease and diabetes: a large waist, high blood pressure, high blood sugar and high triglycerides.
How the body turns food into energy.
When cancer spreads from where it started to another part of the body.
A common first medicine for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood sugar and is usually taken with meals.
Milligram: a very small unit of weight used for medicine doses. 1,000 mg is 1 gram.
A trained health professional who cares for women during pregnancy and childbirth.
A strong, throbbing headache, often on one side, sometimes with nausea and sensitivity to light.
The loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks.
The heart valve between the upper and lower chambers on the left side of the heart.
Milliliter: a small unit of liquid. A teaspoon is about 5 mL. Use the dosing cup or syringe that comes with the medicine.
A vaccine that protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
Magnetic resonance imaging: a scan that uses a strong magnet and radio waves (not X-rays) to make detailed pictures inside the body.
A disease where the immune system damages the covering of nerves (MS), causing problems with vision, movement and balance.
A contagious virus that causes fever and swollen cheeks and jaw. The MMR vaccine prevents it.
The medical name for a heart attack: heart muscle is damaged because its blood supply was blocked.
Inflammation of the heart muscle, often after a virus. It can cause chest pain, tiredness and an irregular heartbeat.
A nasal spray or shot (brand name Narcan) that can quickly reverse an opioid overdose. Many pharmacies sell it without a prescription.
Feeling sick to your stomach, like you might throw up.
A machine that turns liquid medicine into a mist you breathe in through a mask or mouthpiece.
A test result that did not find what was being tested for. For most tests, negative is good news.
A doctor who treats kidney disease.
A thread-like fiber that carries messages between the brain and the rest of the body.
A doctor who specializes in the brain, spinal cord and nerves.
Damage to nerves, often in the hands and feet, causing numbness, tingling or pain.
A baby in the first 28 days of life.
The addictive chemical in tobacco and most vapes. It raises heart rate and blood pressure.
Heavy sweating during sleep that soaks your clothes or sheets.
A medicine for chest pain (angina), often a small tablet placed under the tongue or a spray. It opens up blood vessels quickly.
A small lump of tissue, for example in the lung or thyroid. Many are harmless but may be watched with scans.
A test or treatment that does not cut the skin or go inside the body.
The range of test results found in most healthy people. A result outside it is not always a problem, but your doctor may look closer.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen or naproxen. It eases pain and swelling but can upset the stomach and raise blood pressure.
Loss of feeling in part of the body. Sudden numbness on one side of the body can be a sign of stroke.
A trained health professional who cares for patients, gives medicine and teaches about health. A registered nurse is called an RN.
A nurse with advanced training who can examine patients, diagnose illness and prescribe medicine.
A place where people live who need nursing care and help with daily activities around the clock.
Substances in food that the body needs to live and grow, such as protein, vitamins and minerals.
The panel on packaged food that lists calories, fat, sodium, sugar and other nutrients per serving.
A doctor who cares for pregnancy, childbirth and women's reproductive health (obstetrician-gynecologist).
Having a lot of extra body fat, which can raise the risk of diabetes, heart disease and other problems.
When you stay in the hospital but are not formally admitted. It can change what Medicare and insurance pay, so ask which status you are under.
Therapy that helps people do everyday tasks such as dressing, cooking and bathing after an illness or injury.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder: unwanted repeated thoughts (obsessions) and urges to do things over and over (compulsions).
A greasy cream that holds medicine and is put on the skin.
Take the medicine at least one hour before or two hours after eating.
A doctor who specializes in treating cancer.
When symptoms or a disease began.
Any surgery where the chest is opened to operate on the heart, such as bypass surgery or valve replacement.
A medical doctor who treats eye diseases and does eye surgery.
A strong pain medicine, such as oxycodone, hydrocodone or morphine. It can be addictive and can slow breathing; take only as prescribed.
An eye care professional who checks vision and prescribes glasses and contact lenses.
Surgery to replace a failing organ, such as a kidney or liver, with a healthy one from a donor.
Having to do with bones, joints and muscles.
The most common type of arthritis: the cartilage that cushions joints wears down over time, causing pain and stiffness.
Bones that are thinner than normal but not as thin as in osteoporosis.
A condition where bones become thin and weak and break more easily. Common in older adults.
A middle ear infection, very common in children. It causes ear pain and sometimes fever.
Doctors or hospitals that do not have a contract with your insurance plan. Using them usually costs you more.
The most you will have to pay for covered care in a year. After you reach it, your insurance pays 100% of covered costs.
Care where you go home the same day without staying overnight in the hospital.
Surgery where you go home the same day.
One of two organs in women that make eggs and the hormones estrogen and progesterone.
OTC: medicine you can buy without a prescription.
Taking more of a drug or medicine than the body can safely handle. Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).
How much oxygen your blood is carrying, usually measured with a clip on the finger (pulse oximeter). A normal level is about 95 to 100 percent.
Breathing extra oxygen through a tube under the nose or a mask, for people whose blood oxygen is low.
A small device placed under the skin that helps the heart keep a steady beat.
Care that eases pain and other symptoms and improves comfort for people with serious illness, at any stage.
Feeling your heart racing, pounding, fluttering or skipping beats.
An organ behind the stomach that makes insulin and digestive juices.
A disease outbreak that spreads across many countries and affects many people.
A sudden rush of intense fear with a pounding heart, sweating, shaking or trouble breathing. It can feel like a heart attack; if you are not sure, get checked.
A test that collects cells from the cervix to check for cancer or changes that could become cancer.
A trained emergency worker who gives urgent medical care on the way to the hospital.
A living thing that lives on or inside another, such as lice or worms, and can cause illness.
A brain disease that slowly gets worse and causes shaking, stiffness, slow movement and balance problems.
A secure website or app where you can see test results, message your doctor and make appointments.
Your rights as a patient, such as the right to an interpreter, to understand your care, to refuse treatment and to see your medical records.
An agreement to pay a medical bill in smaller amounts over time. Many hospitals and doctors offer one if you ask.
A doctor who specializes in caring for babies, children and teenagers.
The ring of bones at the base of the spine that connects to the legs; also the lower part of the belly.
One of the first and most common antibiotics. Some people are allergic to it.
A sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. It can cause burning stomach pain.
Inflammation of the thin sac around the heart. It often causes sharp chest pain that gets worse when lying down or breathing in.
Narrowed arteries in the legs or arms (PAD), usually from plaque buildup. It can cause leg pain when walking.
A scan that uses a small amount of a radioactive tracer to show how organs and tissues are working. It is often used to look for cancer.
A trained expert who prepares and gives out medicine and can answer questions about how to take it.
A store or counter where prescription and other medicines are sold.
A trained worker who takes blood samples.
When a doctor or nurse checks your body by looking, listening, and feeling, such as listening to your heart and lungs.
A licensed professional who helps people move better and recover strength after injury, surgery or illness.
Treatment with exercise and hands-on care to help you move better and recover from injury or surgery.
A licensed health professional (PA) who examines, diagnoses and treats patients, working with doctors.
A box with sections for each day (and time of day) to help you take medicines on schedule.
A pea-sized gland at the base of the brain that controls many other glands and hormones.
Heel pain caused by an irritated band of tissue on the bottom of the foot. It is often worst with the first steps in the morning.
A fatty, waxy buildup inside an artery wall that narrows it. In the mouth, plaque is a sticky film of germs on the teeth.
The yellowish liquid part of the blood that carries blood cells, nutrients and hormones.
Tiny pieces in the blood that clump together to stop bleeding.
An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs, causing cough, fever and trouble breathing.
A vaccine that protects against pneumococcal bacteria, a common cause of pneumonia. It is recommended for adults 50 and older and some younger people.
On a prescription, means 'by mouth': swallow the medicine.
A doctor who treats feet and ankles. People with diabetes often see one for foot checks.
A free, 24-hour helpline for poisonings and medicine mistakes. In the U.S., call 1-800-222-1222.
Harm from swallowing, breathing in or touching something toxic. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or 911.
A small growth on the inside lining of an organ, such as the colon or nose. Most are not cancer, but some colon polyps can turn into cancer, so they are removed.
A small device placed under the skin of the chest so medicines (such as chemotherapy) can be given and blood drawn without a new needle in the arm each time.
A test result that found what was being tested for. For many tests this means you have the condition.
After surgery. Post-op care includes pain control, wound care and follow-up visits.
The weeks and months after giving birth.
Depression after having a baby that is stronger and lasts longer than the 'baby blues'. It is common and treatable.
A mineral that helps nerves, muscles and the heart work. Levels that are too high or too low can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
Preferred provider organization: an insurance plan that lets you see doctors in or out of its network, usually without a referral, but costs less in-network.
Before surgery. Pre-op instructions may tell you when to stop eating and which medicines to stop.
Blood sugar that is higher than normal but not yet high enough to be diabetes. Healthy eating and exercise can stop it from turning into diabetes.
A corticosteroid pill used to calm inflammation in many conditions. Do not stop it suddenly if you have taken it for a while.
A serious condition in pregnancy with high blood pressure and signs of organ damage. Warning signs include bad headaches, vision changes and sudden swelling.
A health problem you had before your health insurance started. Under U.S. law, most plans cannot refuse you or charge more because of it.
A urine or blood test that checks for a hormone made during pregnancy.
When a baby is born before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Premature babies may need extra care.
The amount you pay every month for health insurance.
Checkups and care during pregnancy to keep mother and baby healthy.
Vitamins made for pregnancy, with extra folic acid and iron.
A doctor's written order for a medicine or treatment.
A program, often from a drug company or nonprofit, that gives free or low-cost medicine to people who qualify.
The sticker on your medicine bottle showing your name, the medicine, the dose, how often to take it and refills left. Ask the pharmacist to explain anything unclear.
A bedsore: an injury to skin and tissue from lying or sitting in one position too long.
Care that helps prevent illness or find it early, such as checkups, vaccines and screenings. Many plans cover it at no cost.
PCP: your main doctor for checkups and everyday health problems, who refers you to specialists when needed.
Approval you must get from your insurance before certain treatments, tests or medicines, or it may not pay.
On a prescription, means 'as needed': take the medicine only when you need it, such as for pain, not on a schedule.
Live 'good' bacteria in some foods and supplements that may help digestion.
The likely course or outcome of an illness.
Treatment given to prevent a disease, such as a vaccine or medicine before a trip.
A walnut-sized gland in men, below the bladder, that makes part of the fluid in semen. It often grows larger with age.
Cancer of the prostate gland in men. It is common and often grows slowly.
A nutrient in foods like meat, fish, eggs, beans and nuts that builds and repairs muscles and tissues.
Closer to the center of the body. The elbow is proximal to the wrist.
A blood test for prostate-specific antigen, which can be higher with prostate cancer or an enlarged prostate.
A skin condition that causes thick, red, scaly patches, often on the elbows, knees and scalp.
A medical doctor who treats mental health conditions and can prescribe medicine.
A mental health professional who provides therapy and testing but usually does not prescribe medicine.
Talk therapy: treatment for mental health problems by talking with a trained professional.
Post-traumatic stress disorder: a mental health condition after a frightening or dangerous event, with nightmares, flashbacks and strong anxiety.
A blood clot that has traveled to the lungs (PE). It causes sudden shortness of breath and chest pain and is an emergency.
A doctor who treats lung and breathing problems.
Your heartbeat, felt in the wrist or neck. A normal adult resting pulse is about 60 to 100 beats a minute.
A small clip put on a finger that measures your pulse and the oxygen level in your blood.
A deep, narrow wound from something sharp like a nail. It may need a tetanus shot.
On a prescription, means once a day. Many prescriptions now just say 'daily'.
Keeping people who may have been exposed to a contagious disease apart from others to see if they get sick.
Cancer treatment that uses high-energy beams, like strong X-rays, to kill cancer cells.
The medical field that uses X-rays, scans and other imaging to see inside the body.
A change in the skin's color or texture, such as red spots, bumps or blisters.
The area where patients are watched closely as they wake up after surgery.
The last part of the large intestine, just before the anus, where stool is held.
Blood cells that carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. They contain hemoglobin.
A note from your doctor sending you to see a specialist. Some insurance plans require one.
Getting more of a prescription medicine. Your prescription label shows how many refills are left.
Treatment that helps you regain skills and strength after an illness, injury or surgery.
When a disease comes back or gets worse after improving.
When signs of a disease, like cancer, lessen or go away.
Having to do with breathing and the lungs.
How many breaths you take in one minute. A normal adult rate at rest is about 12 to 20.
The thin layer at the back of the eye that senses light and sends pictures to the brain.
An illness that can follow untreated strep throat and can damage the heart valves for life.
An autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness, often in the hands.
A doctor who treats arthritis and autoimmune diseases.
Something that raises your chance of getting a disease, such as smoking, high blood pressure or family history.
A group of muscles and tendons that hold the shoulder joint in place and let you lift and turn your arm.
Respiratory syncytial virus: a common virus that causes cold-like symptoms but can be serious for babies and older adults. Vaccines and preventive shots are available.
A type of fat found mainly in meat, butter and cheese. Too much can raise LDL ('bad') cholesterol.
A serious mental illness that affects how a person thinks, feels and acts, and may include hallucinations or false beliefs.
Pain that runs from the lower back down the back of one leg, caused by a pinched nerve.
A sideways curve of the spine.
A test to look for a disease before you have symptoms, so it can be treated early.
Asking another doctor to review your diagnosis or treatment plan. It is your right and is common before big decisions.
Medicine that makes you calm, relaxed or sleepy during a procedure.
Sitting a lot and getting little physical activity. A sedentary lifestyle raises the risk of heart disease.
A sudden burst of electrical activity in the brain that can cause shaking, staring or loss of awareness.
The body's extreme, life-threatening reaction to an infection. Signs include fever or low temperature, fast heartbeat, confusion and very fast breathing. Call 911.
The amount of food that the nutrition label numbers are based on.
A painful rash with blisters, usually on one side of the body, caused by the chickenpox virus waking up again. A vaccine is recommended for adults 50 and older.
A dangerous condition where not enough blood reaches the organs. Signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, a fast pulse and confusion. Call 911.
Feeling that you cannot get enough air. Sudden or severe shortness of breath is an emergency.
An inherited blood disease where red blood cells are shaped like a sickle (C shape), causing pain, anemia and infections.
An unwanted effect of a medicine or treatment, such as nausea or drowsiness.
Sudden infant death syndrome: the unexplained death of a healthy baby during sleep. Putting babies to sleep on their backs, alone, in an empty crib lowers the risk.
Air-filled spaces in the bones of the face around the nose. Sinus infections cause stuffiness and face pain.
A sinus infection: swelling of the spaces around the nose, causing a stuffy nose, face pain and thick mucus.
Cancer of the skin, usually from sun damage. Melanoma is the most serious kind.
A condition where breathing stops and starts many times during sleep, often with loud snoring. It raises the risk of high blood pressure and heart problems.
Habits that help you sleep well, such as a regular bedtime, a dark quiet room and no screens before bed.
A test, often overnight, that records your breathing, heart rate and brain waves while you sleep. It is used to find sleep apnea.
Prices that go up or down based on your income, used by many community clinics.
Quitting smoking. It lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke within a few years. Free help is available at 1-800-QUIT-NOW.
Having little contact with other people. It is common in older adults and is linked to poorer health.
A professional who helps patients and families with things like insurance, housing, home care and emotional support.
Salt is the main source of sodium in food. Too much sodium raises blood pressure, so people with heart problems are often told to eat less of it.
Pain or scratchiness in the throat, often from a cold or other infection.
A doctor trained in one area of medicine, such as the heart or skin.
Therapy that helps with speaking, understanding language or swallowing, for example after a stroke.
The bundle of nerves that runs down the inside of the backbone, carrying messages between the brain and body.
The backbone: a column of small bones (vertebrae) that supports the body and protects the spinal cord.
A breathing test where you blow hard into a tube to measure how well your lungs work.
An organ on the upper left side of the belly that filters blood and helps fight infection.
A support that holds an injured body part still, often used before a cast or for a sprain.
A stretched or torn ligament (the tissue that holds bones together at a joint), often in the ankle or wrist.
Finding out how big a cancer is and how far it has spread. Stages usually go from 1 (early) to 4 (spread).
A type of medicine (such as atorvastatin) that lowers 'bad' LDL cholesterol and lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Sexually transmitted disease (also called STI): an infection passed through sexual contact, such as chlamydia, gonorrhea or HIV.
A tiny mesh tube placed in a blood vessel to keep it open.
Free of germs. Also means unable to have children.
The tool a doctor uses to listen to your heart and lungs.
Threads used to close a cut or surgical wound. Also called sutures.
A test of a small sample of poop, used to look for blood, infection or signs of colon cancer.
A throat infection caused by strep bacteria, with a very sore throat and fever. It needs antibiotics.
The body's and mind's reaction to pressure or challenges. Long-term stress can harm your health.
A test that checks how the heart works during exercise, usually walking on a treadmill while connected to an EKG. Medicine can be used instead of exercise.
When blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bursts. Signs (BE FAST): face drooping, arm weakness, speech trouble. Call 911 right away.
Help from the government to lower the cost of health insurance, for example through the Health Insurance Marketplace.
When using alcohol or drugs causes problems in a person's life but they cannot stop. It is a treatable medical condition.
Thinking about ending your life. If you or someone you know has these thoughts, call or text 988 or call 911 right away.
Red, painful skin from too much sun. Sunburns raise the risk of skin cancer.
A vitamin, mineral, herb or other product taken to add to your diet. Tell your doctor about supplements because some interact with medicines.
A doctor who does operations.
An unexpected bill, often from an out-of-network doctor at an in-network hospital. U.S. law (the No Surprises Act) protects you from many of these.
When part of the body gets bigger than normal, often from fluid or inflammation.
A change in your body or how you feel that may be a sign of illness, such as pain or fever.
The medical word for fainting: a short loss of consciousness, usually from a drop in blood flow to the brain.
A group of symptoms that happen together and point to a particular condition.
The top number in a blood pressure reading. It measures the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats.
A pill: medicine pressed into a small solid shape.
A heart rate that is faster than normal, usually over 100 beats a minute while resting.
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement: putting in a new aortic valve through a tube in a blood vessel, without opening the chest.
A vaccine that protects against tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough (pertussis). Adults get a booster every 10 years, and during each pregnancy.
When a baby's teeth start to come through the gums, causing drooling, fussiness and chewing.
Seeing a doctor or nurse by video or phone instead of in person.
How hot your body is. Normal body temperature is about 98.6°F (37°C); 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is a fever.
Painful swelling of a tendon, often from overuse.
A tough cord of tissue that attaches a muscle to a bone.
An illness that cannot be cured and is expected to lead to death.
A serious infection from bacteria entering a wound, causing stiff, painful muscles. Prevented by a vaccine every 10 years.
A trained professional who helps with mental health through talking, or with movement and daily tasks through physical or occupational therapy.
When a blood clot forms inside a blood vessel and blocks it.
A gland in the neck that makes hormones controlling energy and metabolism.
On a prescription, means three times a day, often with meals.
A pins-and-needles feeling, often in the hands or feet.
Ringing, buzzing or hissing in the ears when there is no outside sound.
A group of similar cells that work together, such as muscle tissue or skin.
Surgery to remove the tonsils.
Swollen, infected tonsils, causing a sore throat and trouble swallowing.
Two lumps of tissue at the back of the throat that help fight infection.
Put on the skin, such as a cream or ointment.
A tight band wrapped around an arm or leg above a wound to stop severe bleeding.
The windpipe: the tube that carries air from the throat to the lungs.
A surgical opening in the front of the neck into the windpipe, with a tube to help a person breathe.
An unhealthy fat in some fried and packaged foods that raises 'bad' cholesterol and lowers 'good' cholesterol.
A 'mini-stroke' (TIA): stroke signs that go away within minutes or hours. It is a warning sign of a stroke and needs urgent care.
A physical injury, or deep emotional harm from a frightening or painful event.
Sorting patients by how urgent their condition is, so the sickest are seen first.
A type of fat in the blood. High levels raise the risk of heart disease and are measured in a lipid panel.
One of three periods of pregnancy, each about three months long.
A protein released into the blood when the heart muscle is damaged. A blood test for troponin helps diagnose a heart attack.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone. A blood test for TSH is the main check for thyroid problems.
TB: a contagious bacterial infection that usually affects the lungs. Treatable with months of antibiotics.
An abnormal lump of tissue. It can be benign (not cancer) or malignant (cancer).
A type of diabetes where the body makes little or no insulin. People with it need insulin every day.
The most common type of diabetes, where the body does not use insulin well. It is treated with healthy eating, exercise and medicine.
An open sore on the skin or inside the body, such as in the stomach.
A long-term disease that causes inflammation and sores in the lining of the colon, with diarrhea, often bloody.
A scan that uses sound waves to make pictures inside the body, often used during pregnancy.
Not awake and not able to respond. Call 911.
Losing weight without trying. It should be checked by a doctor.
On one side of the body only.
Not having health insurance.
Chest pain that is new, getting worse or happens at rest. It can mean a heart attack is coming and needs emergency care.
One of two tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
The tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
A walk-in clinic for problems that need care today but are not emergencies, such as minor injuries or infections.
A test of your urine to check for infection, kidney problems, diabetes and more.
UTI: an infection in the bladder or urinary tract, causing burning when urinating and needing to go often.
A doctor who treats problems of the urinary tract and male reproductive organs.
The womb: the organ in a woman's lower belly where a baby grows during pregnancy.
A shot or medicine that trains the body to fight a specific disease without getting sick from it first.
Surgery or a procedure to replace a damaged heart valve with a new one made from metal, plastic or animal tissue.
Breathing in vapor from an e-cigarette. Most vapes contain nicotine, which is addictive.
Swollen, twisted veins that you can see under the skin, usually on the legs.
Having to do with blood vessels.
A blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart.
A breathing machine that moves air into and out of the lungs for someone who cannot breathe well enough on their own.
One of the two lower chambers of the heart, which pump blood out to the lungs and body. Also a fluid-filled space in the brain.
A deadly heart rhythm where the lower chambers quiver instead of pumping. It causes cardiac arrest and needs CPR and an AED right away.
The small bones that stack up to form the spine.
A feeling that you or the room is spinning.
A very tiny germ that causes illnesses like colds, flu and COVID-19. Antibiotics do not work on viruses.
Basic body measurements: temperature, pulse, breathing rate and blood pressure.
A substance the body needs in small amounts to stay healthy, such as vitamin C or vitamin D.
Not having enough vitamin B12, which can cause anemia, tiredness and numbness. It is more common in older adults and vegetarians.
Not having enough vitamin D, which can weaken bones. Sunlight, some foods and supplements provide vitamin D.
Throwing up: forcefully bringing up what is in the stomach through the mouth.
The measurement around your waist. A large waist is linked to a higher risk of heart disease and diabetes.
A clinic where you can be seen without an appointment, often in a pharmacy or store, for minor problems.
A blood thinner pill (brand name Coumadin). People who take it need regular blood tests (INR) and should keep the amount of leafy green vegetables they eat steady.
Loss of strength in the body or a part of it. Sudden weakness in the face, arm or leg can be a sign of stroke.
A regular checkup for a child to check growth and development and give vaccines.
A high-pitched whistling sound while breathing, often with asthma.
Blood cells that fight infection. A high count can be a sign of infection.
Pertussis: a very contagious lung infection with violent coughing fits and a 'whoop' sound when breathing in. It is dangerous for babies; a vaccine prevents it.
Take the medicine with a meal or snack, often to protect the stomach or help it work.
Unpleasant physical and mental symptoms when someone stops or cuts back on a drug, alcohol or medicine their body has gotten used to.
Cleaning, protecting and watching a cut, burn or sore so it heals and does not get infected.
A quick picture of the inside of the body, especially bones, made with a small amount of radiation.
